newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Britain discusses Gulf security, Kuwait arm sales.
newsitem.headline: Britain discusses Gulf security, Kuwait arm sales.

text.p: Britain and Kuwait on Tuesday concluded two-days of talks which focused on the tiny Gulf state's ability to defend itself and its acquiring advanced weapons, which London is lobbying hard to supply.

"My visit provided an opportunity to discuss all aspects of our defence relationship," British Foreign Office Minister Derek Fatchett told a news conference before leaving for neighbouring United Arab Emirates.

A $150 million order for British Aerospace Plc Sea Skua missiles which has been blocked by Kuwaiti parliamentary questions and a requirement for artillery were at the centre of the talks, diplomatic sources said.

But Fatchett said: "It would be inappropriate for me to start discussing individual contracts in public...But you can rest assured that we had a very constructive discussion about the general defence relationship."

Diplomatic sources say that both London and Washington have privately expressed to Kuwait their unease with a recommendation by a Kuwaiti military committee to buy Chinese guns, dropping offers by South Africa, the United States and Britain.
They also expressed doubts over the capability of the Chinese 155mm howitzers and their alleged non-compatibility with Kuwait's mainly Western defence systems, they added.
"A point which we have stressed throughout is that our policy objective, one shared by the Kuwaiti government, is to insure that Kuwait has the ability to defend itself.

"To achieve that you need highly-trained, efficient forces; at the same time well-equipped in a coherent and coordinated way," said Fatchett on the first visit to Kuwait by a British minister since the Labour party came to power last month.

Along with the tracked British Desert AS90, Washington is offering Kuwait its M109 A6 Paladin gun .The South African LIW 155mm G6, the only offer for a wheeled system, seems to have been dropped from the competition, industry sources said.

There has been no official announcement but the sources earlier told Reuters a military committee had picked China to equip a Kuwait Land Forces battalion with 18 tracked howitzers with an option for a second battalion.

Kuwait needed up to three battalions of self-propelled guns which experts said could be worth $600 million depending on specification and training. They said Kuwait's long-term total requirement was for up to five battalions.
Fatchett also discussed ways to finalise a deal for Sea Skua missiles to arm eight fast patrol boats ordered from France in 1995 in a contract worth $500 million, diplomatic sources said.

Kuwait told Britain more than a year ago that it would buy British surface-to-surface missiles but the deal is facing problems in parliament which is questioning why a cheaper offer by France for Aerospatiale MM-15 missiles was dropped.
